title: Out of the Crisis
author: W. Edwards Deming
theme: Quality is made by the system that management designs, so lasting improvement requires management itself to transform how it leads.
summary: W. Edwards Deming wrote this book at a time when American industry was losing ground to Japanese competitors. His diagnosis was uncomfortable for executives. The decline, he argued, was not caused by lazy workers or unfair rivals but by the way companies were managed, and only a deep change in management thinking could reverse it.

His central claim is that better quality does not raise costs; it lowers them. When work is done right the first time, rework, waste and delays fall, productivity rises, and the company can offer better products at lower prices, win markets and keep people employed. Quality is therefore a strategy for survival, not an expense.

Deming insists that most problems come from the system, not from individuals. Every process varies. Some variation is built into the system itself, and some comes from special, identifiable causes. Managers who blame people for faults that the system produces only spread fear and confusion. Statistical thinking helps leaders tell the two apart and act on the right one.

He sets out fourteen points for management. Among them: keep a constant purpose of improvement over the long term; stop relying on mass inspection and build quality in from the start; stop choosing suppliers on price alone; improve the system constantly; train people properly; replace slogans, targets and quotas with real leadership; drive out fear; break down barriers between departments; and let people take pride in their work.

He also warns against what he calls deadly diseases, such as chasing short-term profits, judging people through annual ratings, frequent turnover among managers, and running a company only on the figures that are easy to see.
The book's message is that transformation is everyone's job, but it must start at the top and continue for as long as the organisation exists.
takeaway: Stop blaming workers for what the system produces; leaders must improve the system continuously and build quality in from the start.

questions.q: According to Deming, what was the main cause of the crisis facing American industry?
questions.why: Deming placed responsibility on management practices rather than on workers or outside forces.

questions.q: What does Deming say happens to costs when quality improves?
options: Costs fall because rework, waste and delays decrease
Costs rise because better materials are needed
Costs stay the same while prices rise
Costs rise at first and never recover
questions.why: He argued that doing work right the first time cuts waste and rework, which lowers cost and raises productivity.

questions.q: Where does Deming locate most of the problems in an organisation?
options: In the system that management designs
questions.why: He held that the system, not the individual worker, produces most faults.

questions.q: Why does Deming want managers to understand variation statistically?
options: To tell variation built into the system apart from variation with special causes
To eliminate the need for training
questions.why: Distinguishing the two kinds of variation tells managers whether to change the system or address a specific cause.

questions.q: What is Deming's view of mass inspection?
options: It is the best way to guarantee quality
It should be done by outside auditors only
Quality should be built in from the start instead of relying on it
questions.why: Inspection finds defects after they are made; Deming wanted processes that prevent them.

questions.q: How does Deming say suppliers should be chosen?
options: Not on price alone, but with attention to quality and long-term relationships
By choosing as many suppliers as possible for each item
questions.why: He criticised awarding business on price tag alone because it ignores total cost and quality.

questions.q: What does Deming recommend in place of slogans, targets and quotas?
options: Real leadership and improvement of the system
questions.why: He believed exhortations and quotas do not change the system, while genuine leadership does.

questions.q: Which of these does Deming count among the 'deadly diseases' of management?
options: Judging people through annual performance ratings
questions.why: He saw annual ratings and merit reviews as damaging because they blame individuals for system results and breed fear.

questions.q: Why does Deming urge organisations to drive out fear?
options: Because fearful people hide problems and cannot work effectively
Because fear reduces the need for managers
Because fear makes inspection harder to carry out
questions.why: When people are afraid they avoid asking questions or reporting problems, which blocks improvement.

questions.q: Who, according to Deming, must lead the transformation?
options: Top management, with everyone taking part
Front-line workers acting on their own
questions.why: He said transformation is everybody's job but must begin with and be sustained by top management.
